- **Late penalty?** **$25,000**
- **When to prepare?** **Start in early March** (allow at least 4 weeks)

✅ **April 15 – FBAR (FinCEN 114) [If Required]**

- **Who must file?** If your UK business holds **$10,000+ in U.S. accounts at any time**
- **When to prepare?** **Start in early April**

✅ **Wyoming Annual Report & Franchise Tax – Due on Your LLC’s Formation Anniversary**

- **Fee:** **$60 minimum** (or **$0.0002 per dollar** of Wyoming-based assets)
- **When to prepare?** **At least 3-4 weeks before your LLC’s anniversary date**

[4/16/26, 1:48:46 PM] ~ Richy Burns: I'm new here but been in the game a while. My first model was PPL and I probably did over 200 sales calls with roofers. I charged $297 as a setup fee. Most roofers laughed at that amount (meaning they would have happily paid more). But here's the thing...it wasn't the amount they paid up front that determined if they were a decent client (meaning they paid on time, were easy to work with etc). It came down to how established their business was. What I mean is when a roofer had a proper CRM, good looking website (modern), an actual team behind him (not a one man band) then they were mostly good clients because they took their shit seriously. They were real business owners who understand the numbers. They new their cost per acquisition etc. 

The ones still using an excel sheet to track shit and working off a free Gmail account were often the tirekickers or the ones that were unrealistic about results.

So, I would ask questions about their business to find these things out. That helped a lot. ‎<This message was edited>

[4/16/26, 1:59:49 PM] ~ Richy Burns: Also, something I did that worked really well on sales calls was to tell them right out the gates that this was just a conversation and that there was no decision to make on this call. This kept things super casual and actually disarmed them a lot. It kind of created reverse psychology because they're like "why's he not pitching me?". This would allow me to actually close easier through conversation instead of awkward silences and I also closed a ton after the call with a simple 3 day SMS campaign. Day 1 after the call they'd get a text reminding them of the up front fee amount and that it would increase in 2 days. The next day I'd say it'd increase in 24 hours. And the last one said it would increase today to $997. Got a lot of conversions just through this approach.

[4/17/26, 3:26:59 AM] ~ Richy Burns: If an Avg job for a contractor is $20k and at 35% margin that’s about $7k profit per deal for them. If we charge $300 per appointment and they close 1 in 10, they’re spending $3k to make $7k, so they’re still up $4k (about 2.3x). 

If they’re closing 1 in 5, they’re spending $1.5k to make $7k, so they keep $5.5k (around 4.7x). 

At $200 per appointment, 1 in 10 means $2k spend for $7k back, so $5k profit (3.5x). And at 1 in 5, it’s $1k spend for $7k back, so $6k profit (7x). 

What this means is at the worst case scenario where you're charging the most/appt and getting the worst results (client only signing 1 job every 10 appts), the client STILL more than doubles their money. Best case they make a 7x or higher. It's a no brainer. 

When i was doing these sales calls I actually built a calculator that i filled in with them on the call. I'd input the standard numbers but afterwards I'd even put in the worst case to show them they can't lose. That means it's not me convincing them - it's the data.

Also, everything is relative, so on avg, it may take more appts to close a new pool deal but its worth more, so you can justify a higher amount per appt. And the opposite is true.

Spoke with a roofer yesterday who told me he'd be happy paying $400-800 for a showed appt (he only did retail, no insurance work or repairs) so the right clients that know their number are absolutely out there and the ones that say "NO" are the ones you don't want to work with anyway (assuming you did a good job of pitching the offer)
